_what: The Pile, a junk playground on the street, built by tools/make-the-pile.py: the Pile itself, the parts you can make something out of, where junk playgrounds come from, the old telly on the Pile and its rack. Ryan Boren's brief, 2026-10-05: a junk or adventure playground of duct tape, fabric, bubble wrap, sand, old wooden furniture, tempera paint, plywood pieces, pallets, pianos, buckets, shovels, ropes, tree stumps and old playground equipment, with our Play page's heading Play Is Learning, and six pages to read.
_light: The den in the middle of the Pile is roofed with bubble wrap, and every bubble throws a ring of light on the sand under it. Nothing else on the Pile is lit by anything but the sun, and the light has no colour in it: all the colour on the Pile is paint.
_parts: Ryan's list, every one of them, in his order. Each says what it is like and some of the things it has been, and none of them is for anything in particular: what a part is on the Pile is whatever whoever is playing says it is. The tool holds one drawing per part and refuses a part it cannot draw. Tempera is written as tempera: the brief's word was tempura, which is a batter.

_history: Every fact here was read on its own page on 2026-10-05. Where two of Wikipedia's articles disagree, the room says so rather than choosing.

history.say: The idea is a Danish landscape architect's, Carl Theodor Sørensen's, who wrote in 1931 about a junk playground where children could make their own world out of what was lying about.

The first was set up in Emdrup, in Denmark, during the German occupation. Wikipedia's article on adventure playgrounds says 1943, and its article on Sørensen says 1940; we have not read anything that settles it.

Lady Allen of Hurtwood, a landscape architect, brought the idea to Britain after the war, to the bomb sites, in a book of 1946 called Why Not Use Our Bomb Sites Like This? There the name changed from junk playground to adventure playground, to make it easier for councils to say yes to.
They are staffed by playworkers, and playwork, in Wikipedia's words, is the work of creating and maintaining spaces for children to play.
The one at the Berkeley Marina opened in 1979 and is still there.
The Land, at Plas Madoc in Wales, seven miles south of Wrexham, has been open since 2011, and Erin Davis made a film about it, The Land, in 2015.
The Yard, on Governors Island, is New York's only adventure playground, and grown-ups stay outside the main area so the children can play their own way.
The idea under all of them has a name, the theory of loose parts, from the artist Simon Nicholson in 1971.

_quotes: Our own Play page's words are checked against the Knowledge System mirror's copy of it word for word on every build when the mirror is there, the Town Hall's rule. The other two are read on the pages named. The cap is forty words, raised from the Zibaldone's thirty on purpose: Simon Nicholson's sentence, the one the theory of loose parts is quoted by, runs to thirty-one, and cutting it would be pedantry dressed as rigour, Covenstead's reason.
